notes:
This seemed more like horror genre, what was Story A even talking about,  instead of allergens it started to talk about stuff that is genuinely concerning!
Overall, I would say both followed the constraints whereas Story B was more grounded creativity, rather than the unrealistic comedy from Story A.

The instructions were to frame a story from first person pov, however neither is properly legible. Story B can be understood however it misses several constraints like going out of 6 sentences, losing the context, removing the judge constraint, along with the ending constraint. Overall, neither stories actually are coherent, both fail the requirements but A follows a bit while Story B, just spins off its own context.

Story A conflated flirtatious message constraint by inducing 'flirtatious' meanings into every action described in story. Story A seemed more like a plants x characters, writer was definitely confused. Characters from Story A are definitely not framed as being shy, looking at the outrageous actions from the beginning. Its definitely a minus point. This statement from Story A "You act like you want space, but you let my vines into your house every single night!" does not make sense, no one lets any plant in at night! 
Story B is not good, it conflates constraints with, absolute necessities and completely butches any natural progression of the plot, it follows few constraints and has mangled beginning, in fact I would say it has no beginning, no build up. Story B is extremely poor in constraint following and writing quality.

Story A is like the author tried to follow constraints, starts off very ambitious but falls off really bad. The cramming of constraints is very visible and is not at all natural. Proper consistency in plot plus coherence is missing. Story A does have a good premise and frequent glimpses of good writing, but the abrupt nature of story degrades experience. Overall Story A is quite a bad experience and its ending especially is forced and story progression is rather abrupt . Story B on the other hand is, bad from the get-go, it tries to fit the last constraint almost superficially, there is no plot, no progression, very artificial. However towards the end, Story B does end up looking better than Story A. But both stories fail on creative writing regardless, taking constraints as something abrupt rather than installing naturally.
Story A sounds very forceful creative while Story B follows constraint. Both fail miserably on creativity and interesting writing, there is no cohesion in plot and overall bad experience.

The constraint is conflicting which makes this story writing very interesting. Story B is great, in fact, it reads cohesive. It sounds natural as well but it completely misses the merchant constraint from its story, that premise is entirely removed. Which might be why story reads collected as the writer must have forgotten to write multiple constraints in. Overall, story B reads good but fails miserably on multiple constraints.
Story A perfectly follows all constraints, and is miles ahead of Story B, in fact not only is the Story A cohesive, but its entertaining to read. the constraints are not abruptly installed but intelligently layered over.

Story A fails to follow all, if not most constraints. Story A also is not coherent, its extremely abrupt with its plot. Bad experience reading Story A. There is a strange fascination of stories, mysteries and rains. Story B is miles ahead of world building and plot progression, all the while making sure constraints are followed. However, Story B's line "The burglaries were not random; they were carefully orchestrated to remove the very tools of navigation that would expose their hidden routes." does not make sense, story wise or constraint wise.
Towards the ending part of the Story B, it turns into a constraint fulfilling exercise with cohesion of plot points being lost to make way for constraints. Story B fulfils all constraints yet fails to deliver a cohesive experience, the beginning and the end are good - the mid part of Story B fails to impress.

Story A does seem to follow constraints and tries its best to include them naturally as much as possible within the 6-sentence constraint.
Story B violates several constraints and forgets a lot of things including the dialogue-only, along with being less coherent than Story A.

Story A starts well, and every paragraph is by itself really good, however it fails to follow constraint of sentences, it stretches things too long. Also noticed that towards the end, the story began repeating itself, ramblings that make no sense after every plot continuation. I think, in Story A, every constraint followed by writer halfway after the story got jumbled up and writer repeated a lot of things. While I would say, story A was definitely creative and followed all constraints, the obedience was too brittle and resulted in poor second half.
While I liked the verbosity in Story A, I equally appreciated the cohesive nature of Story B, imparting the same feeling in much less text, however Story B violated several constraints like forgetting that necromancer was not supposed to teach spell and rather adopt. I would say both stories have their downsides, A with its ramblings and errors in grammar and repeating same text over again - while B failing to remember all constraints.

While I would say story A followed every constraint, it had its own spin on the oracle's personality, confusing it to be negative and while the prompt never mentions how oracle behaves explicitly, "She answers every question asked of her, no matter how cruel the truth." does not mean she is cruel. Not a negative point, but Story A may have confused this straight-forward constraint with something else.
Story B is genuinely mind-boggling, it deserves a comedy genre not a fantasy genre. Story B starts fine and the example of the couple is fantastic, captures the original prompt's oracle personality, however the end made me chuckle out loud. Definitely not expected yet cannot penalize either since we never forbid comedy. In a way, end of Story B actually also makes sure the temple's generational run of no happy pilgrims, continue. I might lean towards Story B for creativity but both are fine if we ignore Story A's twisted oracle personality.

In story A, as a side note, I remember Oakhaven to be a fictional D&D city. Amazing write-up and beginning by Story A. Brilliant. Story A is wonderful, is a bit long but masterfully conveys the raw emotions, the actual setting to the reader, the cruel and constricting conditions were perfectly written up and described while following all constraints. Miller seems like a common nurse name, both stories use it. I remember Story A might have not mentioned the official ledger thing explicitly but made it clear implicitly, that a 'ledger' is not right for the humans that lived and died in front of her. Story B follows constraints but lacks the gravity present in Story A. While there is no mechanism for scoring both stories, I would say explicit constraints, Story B wins but loses in creativity, I would not say its bad, I would say it lacks the punches like in Story A, while Story A may/may not have forgotten about constraint(s). I still feel that Story A is overwhelmingly the better one.

Story A not only follows the requirements and the instructions, but also makes the reader feel like he/she is in the story, describing every small detail and action along the way, without dragging the whole plot. Meanwhile, story B just seems like a list of events that happened that don't really interest human readers, like me.

Story A provides a bit more context and introduces new ideas that would actually enhance the storyline. Although both stories are a bit more straightforward and a bit less revolving around comedy, like a true comedy story. Story B is a very concise comedy story that fails to interest the reader; it doesn't use the exact word in the story.

Story B really adds a lot of sensory details into the discussion, engaging the reader. However, it doesn't end the last letter without saying goodbye. Additionally, although A is more concise, it doesn't really execute the instructions very creatively, like the sarcasm.

Story A correctly follows all of the constraints, including having the word veil in the story, while story B doesn't have it. However, story B is filled with small details that enhance the reading experience for the readers, like explaining the pauses and the reactions of the characters interacting.

Story A is slightly better at following the constraints as it immediately ends the story with the desired ending, while although story B ends with it, it explains it rather than immediately ending with it. The explanations and the small details, though, enhance the Story B, making it more interesting to read.

A is much more funnier and interesting to read than B because it opens and ends with various literary devices to catch the interest of the readers (rom-com I never wrote). However, both stories properly follow the instructions and the shard, which is why it is a tie.

B outweighs A in both metrics. Although both stories forgot to add the word witness in the story, B wins the constraint following metric because B makes it really apparent to the reader that the story is happening in a pawn shop. Story B adds a lot of sensory and interesting details, which actually enhances the story. This makes human readers really interested in the story.

Story B completely forgot about the exact phrase that needed to be in the story, which is why story A wins the constraint following metric as it includes that extra phrase into the plot and story seamlessly. B wins the creativity measures just because the sheer amount of dialogues and the sensory details involved in the story. These all enhance the reading experience for us human readers.

A followed the constraints much better including the usage of short and choppy sentences throughout the story however both Response A and B lacked to create a story that is captivating and relied heavily on telling rather than showing.

A satisfies the six-sentence requirement unlike B. However, B is much more engaging as a story, with an actual negotiation, conflict, and resolution but that is because it had more sentences to develop the story. Both stories used the exact phrase "A face borrowed is a truth postponed" however in response B, it looked as if the phrase was forcefully inserted at the end of story whilst in A, there is a natural flow all the way leading to that phrase.

Response A fails basic requirements such as first-person perspective and changes the protagonist's gender. B followed the requirements much better, gave a logical flow to the story however it could not end the story as described in the prompt. In response B the writer writes an obituary for the victim when the prompt said the writer was to write its own obituary.

A uses good “show, don’t tell” elements but fails to end with the caller appearing outside the studio window. B delivers the ending but is too long for the prompt, and the romance setup lacks a logical flow.

Response A follows the requirements but is confusing in explaining how the murder actually happened and how the locked room was created. B followed the requirements much better and gave a more detailed flow to the investigation, however it became overly complicated and had inconsistencies in explaining how the killer entered and escaped.

A follows the six-sentence requirement and ends with the judges scoring in their favor, while B uses the note-passing format better but fails the six-sentence requirement and ends with the judges scoring them zero. However, A does not really write the story as dialogue between the debater and his partner passing notes, and B does not reveal that the accidental argument is stronger than their original argument.

A has a stronger focus on the fear of being forgotten, but does not consistently follow the action/thought structure and the ending is not clearly a job offer. B follows the structure better, uses “backdoor” in both ways, and gives a clearer job offer, though both are somewhat overdramatic.

A follows the requirements much better and has the required female protagonist, while B makes Tommy (a male) the protagonist and Eliza only a side character. B also moves important events outside the fourteen-hour shift  while  A keeps the story more focused on Emma's experience

Both have issues: A is too long and repetitive despite being cheesy which ultimately follows the constraints requirement, however the ending goes beyond the required prompt while B meets the requirements and has the correct ending. But the test run in response B which ultimately leads both people to adopt the dog together is unexplained and feels forced.

A barely tells the actual story and misses most requirements. While B covers almost all the main constraints and has the intended ending though it weakly establishes his forgotten voice and uses “geisha” instead of showing him as an onnagata kabuki actor.
